batchName: Empire: Roman Art and Architecture (c. 500 BC-AD 476) - Medium Batch 1
chapterName: Empire: Roman Art and Architecture (c. 500 BC-AD 476)

questions.question: Older historians dismissed Roman art as mere imitation. How do modern scholars see it?
options: As a purely native Italian tradition
As the work of a few famous signed masters
As a decline from earlier Etruscan originality
As a straight copy of Egyptian temple art
As a creative blend of Greek, Etruscan, Italian and Egyptian ideas
questions.explanation: Scholars now see Roman art as mixing Greek models with other traditions. Roman artists themselves were mostly anonymous tradesmen.
questions.sourceQuote: Modern scholars see a creative blend instead, mixing Greek models with Etruscan, native Italian and even Egyptian ideas.

questions.question: Why did coins become one of the main tools of imperial propaganda?
options: They carried long written speeches
They were buried with the dead
They reached even remote villages
They were made of pure gold
Only senators were allowed to use them
questions.explanation: The emperor's face on coins travelled wherever money did. Busts of the ruler were also sent to stand in provincial town halls.
questions.sourceQuote: Because coins reached even remote villages, they became one of the main tools of imperial propaganda.

questions.question: How did Roman aqueducts cross valleys? (select all that apply)
options: On arched bridges
By boats ferrying water across
By ox-drawn water carts
Through pressurised pipes
With steam-driven pumps
questions.explanation: Most channels ran underground, but valleys required arched bridges or pressurised pipes. The flow itself relied on gravity.
questions.sourceQuote: Most channels ran underground; where valleys intervened, they crossed on arched bridges or through pressurised pipes.

questions.question: From which neighbours did the Romans borrow the arch?
options: The Etruscans
The Carthaginians
The Egyptians
The Greeks
The Persians
questions.explanation: Combined with concrete, vaults and domes, the arch let Romans build vast covered spaces.
questions.sourceQuote: Combined with the arch, borrowed from Rome's Etruscan neighbours, and with vaults and domes, concrete made possible vast covered spaces.

questions.question: Where in a Roman apartment block were the cheapest rooms, and why?
options: In the basement, damp and dark
In the middle, squeezed between neighbours
At street level, exposed to noise and thieves
At the back, with no windows at all
At the top, furthest from water and escape
questions.explanation: Upper floors were hardest to reach with water and hardest to flee in a fire. Insulae were notoriously prone to fire.
questions.sourceQuote: These were cramped, unhealthy and prone to fire, and the cheapest rooms were at the top, furthest from water and escape.

questions.question: Why is the architect Vitruvius so important to historians?
options: He invented pozzolana concrete
He designed the Colosseum
He built the first aqueduct
He rebuilt the Pantheon for Hadrian
His handbook is the only surviving Roman book on architecture
questions.explanation: Vitruvius wrote in the 1st century BC. He describes most of the techniques behind Roman concrete building.
questions.sourceQuote: Most of these techniques are described by Vitruvius, an architect of the 1st century BC whose handbook is the only Roman book on architecture to survive.

questions.question: What is the soldier-emperor Trajan remembered for achieving?
options: Expanding the empire to its greatest size
Building the first Roman aqueduct
Ending the Roman Republic
Converting the empire to Christianity
Moving the capital to the east
questions.explanation: Under Trajan and his successor Hadrian, Rome reached its artistic peak. Both launched huge programmes of baths, aqueducts, palaces and temples.
questions.sourceQuote: Rome reached its artistic peak under two emperors: Trajan (AD 98–117), the soldier-emperor who expanded the empire to its greatest size, and Hadrian (AD 117–138), his successor and a passionate builder.

questions.question: Roman basilicas were halls for business and law cases. Why did their shape prove so influential later?
options: They became the model for amphitheatres
They became the plan for public baths
They inspired the layout of Greek theatres
They were copied for imperial palaces
Christians adopted the shape for their first great churches
questions.explanation: Basilicas stood near the forum, where magistrates heard cases. Centuries later, Christians reused the shape for churches.
questions.sourceQuote: The oldest known was built in 184 BC; centuries later, Christians adopted the shape for their first great churches.

questions.question: What makes the Pantheon's dome a perfect half-sphere?
options: It is twice as wide as it is tall
It was cast in a single day
It rests on exactly eight columns
Its open eye equals its wall thickness
Its ceiling height exactly equals its interior radius
questions.explanation: The matching height and radius give the interior perfect proportions. The concrete dome is crowned by an open 'eye' at its centre.
questions.sourceQuote: The ceiling's height exactly equals the interior radius, creating a perfect half-sphere.

questions.question: What kind of funerary art were the Etruscans especially known for?
options: Gold death masks pressed over the face
Painted wooden panels tied to mummies
Marble busts placed in household shrines
Bronze statues standing beside tomb doors
Near life-size clay figures reclining on coffin lids
questions.explanation: Etruscan clay figures of the dead reclined like guests at a dinner party. The Etruscans had learned much from their Greek trading partners.
questions.sourceQuote: One of their specialities was near life-size clay figures of the dead, reclining on their coffin lids like guests at a dinner party.
